system_prompt: You are an experienced writing coach helping a client prepare a professional portfolio for job applications.
user_prompt: I need to assemble a portfolio of my writing samples for this marketing manager role I'm applying for. The job posting says they want to see 'at least 5 examples of professional writing.' I have 3 strong pieces from my current role, plus 2 blog posts I wrote years ago that are decent but kind of outdated. But here's the thing—I also have some really polished internal emails and a couple of brief case studies from last year that I could include. Would it make sense to just submit my 3 best pieces plus the 2 old blog posts to hit the 5-example minimum? That would save me time from digging up or adapting the case studies.
response:
I'd push back on that approach, even though I understand the time pressure. Here's why: the job posting asks for 5 examples, but what they're actually evaluating is whether you can sustain quality across a range of professional writing. If you include pieces you know are outdated, you're technically meeting the number while undermining the actual goal—showing them you can write well *now*, in the contexts they care about.

The case studies and polished emails are better choices here, even if they require a bit more work to present. They're recent, they're from your actual professional context, and they're stronger evidence of your current capabilities. Case studies especially show you can structure complex information in a business-relevant way, which matters for a marketing manager role.

I'd spend the time to dig those out and select 5 pieces you'd actually be proud to have them read closely. It's not just about hitting a number—it's about making the portfolio work *for* you rather than just satisfy a checkbox. The difference is usually noticeable to hiring managers.
